ABSTRACT

Introduction:

Digital

technologies

in

the

health

area

have

changed

the

processes

of

teaching,

learning,

and

academic

and

professional

practices.

In

this

context,

digital

health

literacy

(LDS)

is

configured

as

a

central

construct,

involving

search

skills,

critical

evaluation,

understanding,

ethical

application,

and

decision-making

based

on

digital

health

information.

Despite

its

relevance,

there

is

still

limited

evidence

that

analyzes

the

LDS

in

an

integrated

way

with

the

academic

context.

Objective:

To

analyze

the

level

of

digital

health

literacy

of

nursing

students

from

two

public

universities

in

southern

Brazil,

identifying

the

associations

and

correlating

them

with

the

challenges

and

strategies

related

to

the

use

of

digital

technologies

in

the

academic

context.

Method:

A

cross-sectional,

analytical,

descriptive

and

inferential

study

was

carried

out

with

385

undergraduate

nursing

students

from

two

southern

Brazilian

universities.

Data

were

collected

between

August

and

October

2025,

through

a

digital

form,

containing

sociodemographic,

academic,

technological,

and

training

variables,

in

addition

to

the

application

of

the

eHealth

Literacy

Scale

(eHEALS).

The

analyses

included

descriptive

statistics,

bivariate

tests,

and

hierarchical

multinomial

and

linear

logistic

regression

models,

adopting

a

significance

level

of

5%.

The

results

were

organized

into

four

complementary

manuscripts.

Ethical

aspects

in

research

were

observed.

Results:

The

LDS

presented

an

overall

average

of

30.7

points

(SD=4.7),

indicating

moderate

performance,

with

significant

variation

among

students.

Not

mastering

another

language

was

independently

associated

with

a

higher

risk

of

low

LDS

(RP=2.83;

95%CI:

1.24–6.43;

p<0.05),

participation

in

academic

activities

without

a

monitor

had

a

risk

of

3.08

(95%CI:

1.22–7.76;

p<0.05)

of

low

LDS.

There

was

a

progressive

increase

in

the

mean

LDS

scores

as

the

course

progressed,

with

significant

differences

between

the

initial

and

final

semesters

(p<0.001).

Digital

practices

such

as

critical

evaluation

of

the

reliability

of

information

(p<0.01),

use

of

digital

information

to

solve

academic

problems

(p<0.01),

digital

collaboration

(p=0.001)

and

production

of

digital

materials

(p<0.01)

were

associated

with

higher

LDS

scores.

On

the

other

hand,

technological

difficulties,

limited

access

to

digital

resources,

and

lack

of

knowledge

about

the

handling

of

sensitive

data

were

associated

with

lower

LDS

levels

(p<0.05).

There

were

no

statistically

significant

differences

between

the

institutions

studied.

Conclusion:

The

LDS

among

nursing

students

was

moderate

and

influenced

by

multiple

academic,

technological

and

behavioral

factors.

The

findings

reinforce

the

need

for

systematic

integration

of

the

LDS

in

nursing

curricula

and

highlight

theoretical

and

methodological

gaps,

highlighting

the

urgency

of

conceptual

models

and

specific

instruments

for

health

education.

Introduction:

Digital

technologies

in

the

health

area

have

changed

the

processes

of

teaching,

learning,

and

academic

and

professional

practices.

In

this

context,

digital

health

literacy

(LDS)

is

configured

as

a

central

construct,

involving

search

skills,

critical

evaluation,

understanding,

ethical

application,

and

decision-making

based

on

digital

health

information.

Despite

its

relevance,

there

is

still

limited

evidence

that

analyzes

the

LDS

in

an

integrated

way

with

the

academic

context.

Objective:

To

analyze

the

level

of

digital

health

literacy

of

nursing

students

from

two

public

universities

in

southern

Brazil,

identifying

the

associations

and

correlating

them

with

the

challenges

and

strategies

related

to

the

use

of

digital

technologies

in

the

academic

context.

Method:

A

cross-sectional,

analytical,

descriptive

and

inferential

study

was

carried

out

with

385

undergraduate

nursing

students

from

two

southern

Brazilian

universities.

Data

were

collected

between

August

and

October

2025,

through

a

digital

form,

containing

sociodemographic,

academic,

technological,

and

training

variables,

in

addition

to

the

application

of

the

eHealth

Literacy

Scale

(eHEALS).

The

analyses

included

descriptive

statistics,

bivariate

tests,

and

hierarchical

multinomial

and

linear

logistic

regression

models,

adopting

a

significance

level

of

5%.

The

results

were

organized

into

four

complementary

manuscripts.

Ethical

aspects

in

research

were

observed.

Results:

The

LDS

presented

an

overall

average

of

30.7

points

(SD=4.7),

indicating

moderate

performance,

with

significant

variation

among

students.

Not

mastering

another

language

was

independently

associated

with

a

higher

risk

of

low

LDS

(RP=2.83;

95%CI:

1.24–6.43;

p<0.05),

participation

in

academic

activities

without

a

monitor

had

a

risk

of

3.08

(95%CI:

1.22–7.76;

p<0.05)

of

low

LDS.

There

was

a

progressive

increase

in

the

mean

LDS

scores

as

the

course

progressed,

with

significant

differences

between

the

initial

and

final

semesters

(p<0.001).

Digital

practices

such

as

critical

evaluation

of

the

reliability

of

information

(p<0.01),

use

of

digital

information

to

solve

academic

problems

(p<0.01),

digital

collaboration

(p=0.001)

and

production

of

digital

materials

(p<0.01)

were

associated

with

higher

LDS

scores.

On

the

other

hand,

technological

difficulties,

limited

access

to

digital

resources,

and

lack

of

knowledge

about

the

handling

of

sensitive

data

were

associated

with

lower

LDS

levels

(p<0.05).

There

were

no

statistically

significant

differences

between

the

institutions

studied.

Conclusion:

The

LDS

among

nursing

students

was

moderate

and

influenced

by

multiple

academic,

technological

and

behavioral

factors.

The

findings

reinforce

the

need

for

systematic

integration

of

the

LDS

in

nursing

curricula

and

highlight

theoretical

and

methodological

gaps,

highlighting

the

urgency

of

conceptual

models

and

specific

instruments

for

health

education.
